title: War beginning in South Carolina will spread to all nations
setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation on 25 December 1832 at or near Kirtland, Ohio. That autumn South Carolina had declared federal tariffs void and threatened to leave the Union. A nearby newspaper, the Painesville Telegraph, had just reported the crisis along with cholera and plague abroad. Frederick G. Williams recorded the revelation. It was left out of the 1835 and 1844 Doctrine and Covenants and first printed in England in 1851.
summary: The revelation speaks of wars that will begin with the rebellion of South Carolina. It says the Southern States will be divided against the Northern States. The South will call on Great Britain, and other nations will be drawn in until war is poured out on all nations. It says slaves will rise against their masters. It says the remnants left in the land will vex the Gentiles. Famine, plague, earthquake, and lightning will follow until there is a full end of all nations. It closes by telling the Saints to stand in holy places and not be moved until the day of the Lord.

contextNote.title: Standing still amid predicted war
contextNote.text: The revelation asks what the Saints should do while war and disaster spread. Verses 1–6 describe the danger, starting in South Carolina and widening to all nations. Verse 7 gives the stated purpose: to end the cry of the saints against their enemies. Verse 8 tells them to “stand ye in holy places” and not be moved. The command is about steadiness and place, not about joining the fighting. Latter-day Saints later pointed to the Civil War, which began in South Carolina in 1861; the 1832 crisis itself ended without war. In this passage, “holy places” are where the Saints wait for the day of the Lord.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 85–87, “Stand Ye in Holy Places,” takes its title from verse 8. What places, habits, or relationships in your life could help you stand and “be not moved” as verse 8 directs?

newPlaces.name: South Carolina
newPlaces.why: v. 1 names the rebellion of South Carolina, the 1832 Nullification Crisis

reviewNote: Read all 8 verses. Heading gives at or near Kirtland, 25 December 1832, slavery and the nullification context. JSP historical introduction gives the 21 December Painesville Telegraph reports, Williams as scribe, omission from the 1835 and 1844 editions, and 1851 publication in England in the Pearl of Great Price. Great Britain (v. 3) is named but not added as a place. The Civil War sentence is a neutral note on later reception; reviewers may adjust its wording.
